This study examines a cell-free massive MIMO system with multiple antennas at access points and users having multiple antennas. The primary goal is to maximize non-real-time user data rates while ensuring real-time users meet their minimum required data rate. The problem is complex due to the interdependence of variables and non-convex constraints, necessitating a solution via a split convex updatable concave updatable (SCOPE) algorithm. The proposed algorithm uses a two-stage approach, initially applying a sequential fractional programming method to optimize non-real-time user rates and then using a split concave updatable updatable (SCUU) algorithm to optimize real-time user rates. The proposed method is shown to converge and its performance is evaluated through simulations, demonstrating a significant performance gain of up to 15 dB over conventional methods.

Decision trees and deep neural networks are two prominent machine learning methods, each offering distinct advantages. Decision trees provide straightforward explanations, whereas deep neural networks excel in performance. This study presents a novel approach to combining the strengths of both methods by using decision trees to approximate deep neural networks. The proposed technique is evaluated through various experiments, including regression and classification tasks, and is further demonstrated in a real-world application involving the identification of COVID-19 patients from chest X-ray images. The results show that our approach yields decision trees comparable to those of established methods while achieving performance levels similar to those of deep neural networks.

This research introduces a blockchain-based framework for secure, decentralized communication between agents, enabling them to verify message integrity, origin, and authenticity. By leveraging the blockchain's inherent properties, this framework fosters mutual trust among agents, even those with a history of dishonest behavior. An implementation of this framework is demonstrated using a blockchain-based chat application, and its efficacy is showcased through a simulated scenario involving two dishonest agents and one trustworthy agent.

We examine the potential for detecting $\eta$-attractor models in observations, specifically focusing on the impact of higher-order corrections to the $\eta$-expansion. By applying a perturbative approach, we develop a method to determine the validity of the $\eta$-expansion for various scalar potentials, and we demonstrate that it holds true for a broad class of models, including those with exponential and step-like forms. Our analysis reveals that this method can be used to assess the validity of the $\eta$-expansion for a wide range of scalar potentials, and we apply this method to investigate the validity of the $\eta$-expansion for models with double well potentials.

Intel has successfully developed a series of high-performance, many-core processors known as Intel Xeon processors, which are capable of handling complex artificial intelligence tasks. This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of the capabilities of Intel Xeon processors, utilizing a diverse set of benchmarks that encompass a range of machine learning and deep learning applications. The study provides a detailed analysis of the performance of Intel Xeon processors, utilizing both CPU and GPU resources, and compares them to other cutting-edge processors. The findings demonstrate that Intel Xeon processors can achieve exceptional performance in a variety of AI tasks, including image classification, object detection, and natural language processing.

Three standard methods for establishing equivalence include equivalence testing, confidence interval estimation, and TOST, all of which are based on the principle of statistical power. Researchers have developed various approaches to evaluate these methods, including asymptotic analysis and simulation studies. This paper presents an alternative method for analyzing these methods, which involves applying a first-order approximation to the noncentral t-distribution. By doing so, it provides a closed-form solution for approximating the power of these methods, which can be used to compare them and determine their relative performance. The results show that the approximations are accurate, and the proposed method can be used to compare the performance of these methods under different conditions. The paper also provides a simple R function for calculating the power of these methods, which can be used to determine the optimal sample size for each method.

A new approach to semantic image transmission is introduced, leveraging a convolutional neural network to extract meaningful image features. These features are then encoded using a vector quantization scheme, and the selected codewords are transmitted to the receiver. The receiver utilizes a neural network to reconstruct the image from these transmitted features. The proposed system is optimized by adjusting the number of training images and the size of the codebook. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms traditional image compression techniques in terms of semantic quality, and its performance is comparable to a system that transmits the entire image.

In the field of big data analytics, the concept of "explaining results" has gained significant attention. A key challenge lies in the fact that big data analytics models often produce results that are difficult to interpret, particularly when dealing with complex, non-linear models. To address this issue, researchers have proposed "result-aware" approaches, which aim to make the results of big data analytics more understandable. These approaches can be categorized into two main types: post-hoc and result-aware. While post-hoc approaches generate explanations after a model has been trained, result-aware approaches integrate explanation into the model training process. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of result-aware approaches, including their benefits, limitations, and potential future directions.

This research paper introduces a novel statistical model for analyzing complex network data, which can be applied to various fields such as social media, biology, and finance. The proposed model, Bayesian grouped network autoregression, is designed to forecast future network states by considering the influence of existing network connections and the time-dependent trends of individual nodes. By incorporating prior knowledge and accounting for uncertainty, this model provides more accurate predictions and insights into the underlying dynamics of network evolution. The authors develop a computationally efficient approach for estimating the model's parameters and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations and real-world applications, including social media analysis and stock market prediction.

Research has shown that verifying scientific claims is a difficult task, primarily due to the vast amount of information available and the lack of specialized expertise in the field. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes a multi-stage process involving a language model, a scientific question answering model, and a verifier to determine the validity of a given claim. Our method, which we refer to as the Claim Verifier, has been tested on the ScienceQA dataset and has demonstrated a significant improvement in accuracy, achieving a 70.4% accuracy rate compared to the previous best result of 61.1%.

The human eye's cross-sectional images captured by OCT are utilized to segment the eye into its distinct sections, including the front, middle, and rear parts. This segmentation is crucial for diagnosing various eye conditions. A new approach, called the DeepEyeNet, is proposed to automate this process. It uses a deep learning-based method to identify and extract the eye's sections from OCT images. This approach is based on a deep neural network that is trained to recognize and extract the eye's sections from a large dataset of OCT images. The results show that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in segmenting the eye's sections, with an average accuracy of 90.4%. This high accuracy is achieved by using a deep learning-based method that is robust to variations in the eye's structure and is able to accurately identify and extract the eye's sections from a wide range of OCT images.

Cognitive models have been developed to simulate human thought processes, but they often fall short in replicating the dynamic nature of human cognition. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that incorporates time into these models by integrating them with the capabilities of large language models. By leveraging the temporal understanding capabilities of these models, we can create cognitive models that are more accurate and realistic in their predictions of human behavior. Our results show that the dynamic cognitive models outperformed the traditional models in replicating human behavior, suggesting that the dynamic approach has the potential to provide a more accurate representation of human thought processes.

This research delves into the properties of Mersenne primes, introducing the "Eight Levels Theorem" and exploring their connections to other prime numbers. A newly defined function, $Q(n)$, is used to establish a "prime number generator" that identifies potential Mersenne prime factors. Additionally, this study presents a novel approach to solving the Goldbach Conjecture and offers a formula to estimate the number of primes within a given range, ultimately leading to an approximate solution for the prime-counting function.

The Boltzmann equation is a widely applicable model for describing the behavior of dilute gases, and it's used in various fields, including plasma physics, astrophysics, and fluid dynamics. However, extracting hydrodynamic properties from this equation is a complex task, and it's been a subject of research for a long time. This paper presents a novel approach to this problem by using a combination of the Boltzmann equation and a specially designed numerical method. By applying this method, we're able to accurately simulate the behavior of a fluid under different conditions, and we're able to verify the accuracy of our results by comparing them to known solutions. Our results show that this method is effective in capturing the essential features of the Boltzmann equation, and it's a promising approach for solving complex problems in this field.

We introduce a code-switching dataset for Indonesian and English, comprising 1,000 sentences, which we use to evaluate the effectiveness of various methods in separating mixed-language text into its original monolingual components. Our analysis of the dataset's characteristics and annotation challenges, particularly in relation to low-resource languages, is also explored. Furthermore, we assess the performance of multiple methods, including rule-based, neural network, and transformer-based models, on the dataset, and compare their results to the baseline model.

The impact of a star's X-ray radiation on the surrounding disc can lead to the evaporation of gas and dust, resulting in mass loss. This phenomenon is particularly significant for young stars, as their X-ray output is much higher than that of older stars. This study investigates the effect of this mass loss on the disc's structure and evolution, using a detailed model that incorporates the effects of photoevaporation. The model reveals that the mass loss rate can be substantial, reaching up to 10^-9 solar masses per year, and that the mass loss can significantly affect the disc's evolution, particularly for discs with low mass. The study also finds that the mass loss rate is highly dependent on the disc's initial mass and the star's X-ray output, and that the mass loss can significantly reduce the lifetime of a disc, particularly for discs with low mass. The study's findings have important implications for our understanding of the formation of planets and the evolution of protoplanetary discs.

This paper introduces a new family of explicit generalized-$\alpha$ methods that can achieve high-order accuracy for hyperbolic problems. The proposed high-order explicit generalized-$\alpha$ methods are derived by applying the second-order central difference method to the original generalized-$\alpha$ algorithm, resulting in a more efficient and stable numerical solution. The new method's performance is evaluated through a comprehensive analysis of its stability and accuracy, including a detailed stability analysis and numerical experiments that demonstrate its effectiveness. The results show that the new method can achieve high-order accuracy and stability while maintaining a relatively simple implementation.

We investigate the polaron's residue, a key indicator of its integrity, within a Bose-Hubbard polaron model featuring impurities. Our analysis reveals that an increase in impurity-bath interactions leads to a corresponding decrease in polaron residue, accompanied by the emergence of a critical impurity-bath coupling threshold beyond which polaron integrity is lost. Furthermore, we explore the polaron's mass and its dependence on the impurity-bath interactions, uncovering a corresponding decrease in mass as the impurity-bath coupling increases.

In the event of a hurricane, the demand for essential supplies can be unpredictable and change rapidly, making it difficult to meet the needs of affected areas. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach that leverages machine learning to forecast the demand for relief items in real-time. By analyzing historical data and incorporating contextual factors, our model can accurately predict the demand for specific items in specific regions during a hurricane. We have tested our approach using real-world data from Hurricane Sandy and achieved significant improvements over existing methods. Moreover, our model can be easily adapted to other types of disasters and different forecasting scenarios.

Pulsar timing array data analysis for signals from supermassive black hole binaries is complicated due to the necessity of precise timing. This paper presents an efficient method for calculating the timing of these signals by using a Fourier series to represent the binary's waveform. The approach is found to be the most effective among those considered, including the use of the Fourier series and a Taylor expansion. The method is tested on a binary with a mass of 1000 solar masses and an orbital period of 10 hours, and the results show that it can calculate the timing of these signals with a precision of 10^-15 seconds within a few seconds of computation time.

In a game where multiple agents with incomplete information interact, each agent's private information is linked to their own action, and they make decisions based on the actions of others. We investigate the scenario where agents can share their private information before making their decisions. We find that if the private information is of low quality, sharing it leads to a unique outcome, whereas sharing it when the private information is of high quality results in multiple possible outcomes, and this is due to the fact that sharing information leads to a more accurate understanding of the game, and this is more likely to occur when the private information is of high quality.

The COVID-19 pandemic has severely impacted the global economy, necessitating urgent action to mitigate its effects. In response, a novel risk assessment tool has been developed, leveraging artificial intelligence to provide accurate predictions and actionable insights. This study proposes a COVID-19 risk assessment model that integrates the power of deep learning and machine learning techniques. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to accurately forecast the disease's spread, as evidenced by a high correlation coefficient of 0.99. The model's performance is further validated by its ability to accurately predict the disease's spread in multiple countries, including China, Italy, and the United States. The proposed model's accuracy is also showcased through its ability to accurately predict the disease's spread in a specific region, as demonstrated by a correlation coefficient of 0.99. The study's findings have significant implications for public health policy and risk management, as they provide a reliable tool for predicting the disease's spread and informing policy decisions.

A novel multi-resolution SPH technique is introduced to enhance fluid-structure interactions. The method incorporates a multi-resolution framework, allowing for the integration of SPH particles with a fixed Eulerian grid. The grid is used to model solid boundaries and facilitate particle reinitialization, while a novel SPH-to-grid interpolation method enables pressure forces to act on particles near boundaries. The scheme is validated through simulations of fluid-structure interactions, including flow around a stationary cylinder and a flexible plate, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving energy conservation and accurate flow behavior.

Topological insulators are characterized by unique transport properties, including the presence of topologically protected surface states. The topological classification of materials can be determined by analyzing the topological invariants of their Bloch Hamiltonian. However, this approach is not applicable to materials with disorder. This study presents a method for calculating the topological invariants of disordered materials using the wave function of the system's ground state. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective for both two-dimensional and three-dimensional models, including the Haldane model and a three-dimensional topological insulator model. The results show that the wave function method yields the same topological invariants as the clean material, even in the presence of disorder. This approach is applicable to any material with a gapped bulk and can be used to determine the topological invariants of disordered materials.

The High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will be the next phase of the Large Hadron Collider, a groundbreaking particle accelerator. The HL-LHC's design is set to be operational by 2029, and the CERN Scientific Steering Committee has approved its development. The SSC Review Panel's report will be the culmination of a comprehensive review process that will take into account the design and operation of the HL-LHC, and the SSC Review Panel's report will be the final word on its approval. We examine the ergodicity of mean-type mappings derived from a specific function $F$ defined on the positive real numbers. This function satisfies a particular condition, where the sign of a certain expression involving $x$, $y$, and $F(x,y)$ depends on whether $x$ is greater than or less than the geometric mean of $x$ and $y$.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of thermal OH emission in the outer Galaxy, using a novel approach that combines data from the Green Bank Telescope and the Very Large Array. Our analysis has revealed a substantial amount of molecular gas in the outer Galaxy, with a total mass of approximately 1.5 billion solar masses, and a density of around 100 solar masses per parsec cubed. Our findings suggest that the outer Galaxy is characterized by a complex structure, with a significant portion of its molecular gas distributed in a disk-like shape. Furthermore, we have found that the outer Galaxy is a site of active star formation, with a significant portion of its molecular gas converted into stars at a rate of approximately 0.005 solar masses per year. Our results also indicate that the outer Galaxy is a site of active star formation, with a significant portion of its molecular gas converted into stars at a rate of approximately 0.005 solar masses per year.

In a model of an economy with multiple sectors, we examine how consumer preferences impact wage levels and the distribution of income. Our analysis reveals that wages vary across sectors, and income disparities can be significant. Furthermore, we find that consumer preferences can give rise to multiple equilibriums, and the equilibrium with the highest level of aggregate income may not coincide with the one that is socially optimal.

We investigate the phase behavior of a two-dimensional system of active particles with a head and tail structure, where their movement characteristics are influenced by a parameter that can be adjusted. By varying this parameter, we observe a transition from a disordered state to a state of polar order, which is a second-order phase transition. This transition is accompanied by a change in the system's behavior, from a state of criticality to a state of jamming. By analyzing the system's behavior, we find that it exhibits a crossover between these two states, which is a unique feature of this system. This behavior is in contrast to other active matter systems, where the phase transition is typically a first-order transition. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of active matter systems and their potential applications in various fields, including biology and materials science.

We have calculated the decay width of the $\Xi_{cc}^{+ +} \to \Xi_c^+ e^+ \nu_e$ process, which involves the transition from the ground state to the first excited state. Our analysis utilized the QCD sum rules approach, incorporating the light-cone sum rules method to determine the necessary form factors. We have also evaluated the semileptonic branching fraction for the $\Xi_{cc}^{+ +} \to \Xi_c^+ e^+ \nu_e$ process, which is approximately $1.1 \times 10^{-5}$.

In a cooperative setting, a sensor network collaborates to locate an object of interest. This research examines a specific configuration where two sensors, Observer and Locator, work together. The Observer gathers data on the object's position, while the Locator determines its own location using a communication link with the Observer. A novel approach is proposed to estimate the object's position, accounting for the Locator's location uncertainty. A mathematical model is established to analyze the performance of this method, and its accuracy is validated through simulations.

Vibration analysis is a crucial tool for diagnosing rotating machinery issues, and its effectiveness relies heavily on the quality of data collected. However, the presence of noise in this data can significantly impede the accuracy of diagnoses. To address this challenge, a novel method has been developed to assess the reliability of data collected from rotating machinery. This method, known as the Band Relevance Factor (BRF), is based on the analysis of data frequency bands and their respective contributions to overall signal energy. By applying BRF to data collected from various machinery components, the method can identify and eliminate noisy data, thereby improving the accuracy of diagnoses. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing diagnostic performance.

Our investigation into the superconducting properties of CaPtSi3 and CaIrSi3 using muon-spin relaxation has revealed that these materials exhibit spin singlet pairing with a symmorphic s-wave symmetry. Notably, CaPtSi3 displays an isotropic superconducting gap, whereas CaIrSi3 exhibits a highly symmetric superconducting gap, albeit with a small two-gap feature. The observed characteristics of these materials are consistent with the predictions of the kagome band structure, which is a key factor in their superconducting behavior.

A novel approach to solving optimal control problems is presented, leveraging a sparse grid to approximate the value function. The method's efficiency is demonstrated through numerical examples, showing that the sparse grid yields comparable results to the dense grid while significantly reducing computational time.

A novel approach to estimating density functions is introduced, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics. This method, grounded in the quantum central limit theorem, is an unbounded variant of the classical central limit theorem. Its efficacy in machine learning is demonstrated through applications in density estimation, novelty detection, and anomaly detection. Quantum computing capabilities are utilized to accelerate the convergence rate, yielding a significantly improved result compared to its classical counterpart. This research also explores the potential for optimizing this method using quantum annealing techniques.

To effectively decarbonize the electric power sector, a new control strategy is required that can handle the complexities of a decentralized power grid with diverse energy sources and storage systems. Existing control methods, which rely on a hierarchical structure, have limitations in terms of scalability and efficiency, hindering their ability to achieve carbon neutrality. To address this challenge, a novel control framework is proposed that leverages the unique properties of a specific type of network topology, enabling decentralized decision-making and optimal resource allocation. This approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a diverse energy mix, including renewable energy sources and storage systems, and shows that the proposed method can achieve the same level of performance as traditional centralized control methods, while offering improved scalability and flexibility.

We've developed a new, two-dimensional percolation model that incorporates a unique, fractal-like structure. This model is characterized by the presence of a percolating cluster, which is comprised of a backbone and a self-similar, branching framework. The branching process is governed by a fractal dimension, $D$, and the connectivity of the backbone is defined by a power-law distribution. By employing a combination of numerical simulations and analytical methods, we've investigated the properties of this model, including its fractal dimension, critical exponents, and the relationship between them. Notably, our findings reveal that the fractal dimension of the percolating cluster is directly related to the fractal dimension of the branching process, and that the critical exponents of the model exhibit a non-trivial dependence on the fractal dimension of the backbone.

Achieving optimal performance in catalytic fixed bed reactors is heavily reliant on precise temperature management. This study focuses on developing a model predictive control strategy to regulate temperature distribution within a fixed bed reactor. A novel approach involves utilizing a reduced-order model to forecast temperature profiles, which are then optimized using a dynamic optimization method. This method leverages a combination of a reduced-order model and a dynamic optimization algorithm to ensure efficient and effective temperature management. This approach is demonstrated through a case study involving an exothermic reaction, showcasing its potential to effectively manage temperature profiles within the reactor.

The superconducting behavior of a material is defined by a series of distinct, opposing states that are triggered by an external magnetic field. A notable characteristic of a certain compound, CeRhIn5, is that superconductivity reappears when the magnetic field is increased, a phenomenon known as superconducting reentrance. A recent study on CeRhIn5 under high pressure reveals that this unique behavior persists even when the material is subjected to pressures up to 10 gigapascals. Furthermore, our findings indicate that this behavior is closely linked to a specific, intermediate state that is characterized by a unique, non-orthogonal magnetic structure.

This research introduces a deep Q-learning-based approach to optimize ultra-wideband (UWB) communication, focusing on enhancing packet reception rates and minimizing energy consumption. A deep Q-network is designed to learn the optimal action-value function, considering the UWB channel's state, and the agent's actions are determined by the network's output. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated through simulations, demonstrating its ability to achieve higher packet reception rates and lower energy consumption compared to conventional UWB communication systems.

We examine the k-median problem under the L1 norm in two-dimensional space, focusing on the Euclidean metric. This problem is known to be NP-hard, but we explore whether it can be solved in polynomial time when the number of facilities (k) is fixed. We show that the k-median problem under the Euclidean metric is solvable in polynomial time for a given k, but we also prove that the same problem under the Chebyshev metric is NP-hard.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning is an area of study that has gained significant attention in recent years, primarily due to its potential to solve complex problems that single-agent reinforcement learning cannot. However, multi-agent reinforcement learning faces challenges such as the exponential increase in action spaces and the interdependence of agents. To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach called the Multi-Agent Actor-Critic algorithm with a novel reward decomposition method. This method utilizes a combination of value decomposition and a new reward decomposition technique to facilitate cooperation among agents. Our approach also incorporates a novel reward decomposition method that allows agents to learn from their own rewards while still taking into account the rewards of other agents. This enables agents to learn from their interactions with the environment and other agents, ultimately leading to improved performance. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in solving complex problems in multi-agent reinforcement learning, as evidenced by its successful application in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge.

We have developed a propositional translation for first-order logic of regularities (FroL) that maps first-order formulas to sets of propositional variables, and we have established that this mapping yields an upper bound on the computational complexity of satisfiability checking in FroL that is exponential. This outcome is significant because it resolves a long-standing open problem regarding the computational complexity of FroL, and it also provides insight into the expressiveness of FroL, which is capable of simulating the satisfiability problem of first-order logic. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that FroL is expressively equivalent to the modal mu-calculus with regularities, and we have shown that this equivalence is achieved through a FroL to mu-mCR and a mu-mCR to FroL translation. This equivalence is significant because it allows us to leverage the expressiveness of FroL in order to reason about properties of mu-mCR, and it also provides a new understanding of the expressiveness of mu-mCR.

This paper presents a novel Bayesian approach to solving the linear inverse problem, specifically tailored for signals and images. Building on existing methods, we introduce a flexible Bayesian framework that can be applied to any prior distribution, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by incorporating a sparsity-inducing hyperprior. The resulting model is solved using a variational Bayesian algorithm, and we evaluate its performance on a range of image restoration tasks, including denoising, deblurring, and super-resolution. The results show that our approach outperforms existing methods, and we provide a detailed analysis of its computational efficiency and scalability.

The issue of air quality monitoring in urban areas is addressed by adopting a
data collection strategy that utilizes mobile devices, known as drive-by sensing.
This approach involves collecting data from vehicles moving through the city,
which can be more efficient and cost-effective than traditional stationary
monitoring methods. However, the data collected from vehicles may not cover all
areas of the city, leading to potential gaps in air quality measurements.
This paper proposes a novel approach to optimize the data collection process
by selecting a limited number of vehicle trajectories that minimize the air
quality estimation error. The problem is formulated as a complex optimization
task that involves balancing multiple objectives, including vehicle movement
constraints and data quality. To address this challenge, a novel solution
method is developed that combines a novel optimization technique with a
machine learning model to predict air quality. The proposed approach is
evaluated through simulations and real-world data analysis, and the results show
that it can significantly improve air quality estimation accuracy compared to
existing methods.

We define a specific Weil representation, denoted as $\Delta$, for the generalized special linear group $G_{m,n}$ associated with the split simple Lie algebra of type $A_{m,n}$. Our approach involves utilizing the generalized theta representation of the Weyl group $W_{m,n}$ to construct a representation, $\Psi$, of $G_{m,n}$, which ultimately allows us to establish a decomposition of $\Delta$ into a sum of $W_{m,n}$-invariant irreducible components.

The rapid advancement of AI technology has led to a growing interest in AI-driven persuasive video generation. This field, which combines AI with the power to influence emotions and behaviors, has the potential to revolutionize the way we create and consume media. The ultimate goal of AI-powered persuasive video generation is to create a video that effectively persuades the viewer to take a desired action. This process involves three key steps: (1) understanding the user's needs and preferences, (2) crafting a compelling narrative, and (3) producing a high-quality video. By leveraging AI, these steps can be automated, allowing for the creation of highly personalized and persuasive videos. This paper provides an overview of the current state of AI-powered persuasive video generation, highlighting the key challenges and opportunities in this field.

We introduce an efficient method for designing a time-dependent Hamiltonian that accurately replicates the desired final state of a trapped ion system, using the time-dependent variational principle. This approach is validated by its ability to create precise single-qubit and two-qubit gates, as well as simulate complex many-body dynamics. Notably, our method can be applied to trapped ions, superconducting qubits, and other quantum systems, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical simulations.

The development of complex computational models in neuroscience has been hindered by the need to explore extensive parameter spaces, which can be achieved through the use of high-performance computing. A new approach to modeling the human brain's cortex has been proposed, incorporating a novel method for simulating large-scale networks of neurons. This approach, known as the Neural Mass Model, has been successfully implemented on a high-performance computing platform, allowing for the simulation of complex brain networks with a high degree of accuracy. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of this method to provide valuable insights into the brain's function and behavior, and to inform the development of new treatments for neurological disorders.

We introduce CAMO++ as a comprehensive camouflaged instance segmentation dataset, featuring 10,000 diverse images and corresponding masks and labels. This dataset is comprised of 5,000 newly annotated images and 5,000 images from the original CAMO dataset. The new annotations include precise camouflaged object labels, significantly surpassing the original dataset's accuracy. To assess the performance of camouflaged instance segmentation methods, we have developed a new evaluation metric called the average precision at 0.5 (AP0.5). This metric is more accurate than the average precision at a threshold of 0.5 (AP0.5) in distinguishing between similar objects. To facilitate further research, we have also released a set of baseline models, including CAMONet++, a more advanced version of CAMONet, and CAMO++-V2, a refined version of the original CAMO model. These models demonstrate notable improvements in performance, with the new CAMONet++ model achieving a 10% increase in the average precision at a threshold of a specific value.

We have explored the impact of Lorentz violation on superconductors with the help of the Proca model, which is used to describe photon behavior. By modifying the action to include a preferred frame, we have found that it leads to observable changes in the properties of superconductors. Specifically, our analysis shows that the Lorentz violation alters the depth at which magnetic fields penetrate the superconductor, affects the critical magnetic field, and changes the behavior of vortices within the material.

A major shortcoming in current AI model evaluation is its reliance on standardized benchmarks, which are often insufficiently diverse and fail to capture real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method that leverages user feedback to pinpoint AI model shortcomings. Our method involves collecting and analyzing user-generated examples of AI model failures, which we then use to create targeted datasets for evaluation. By applying this approach to various AI models, we are able to identify and categorize specific failure modes, including those related to specific tasks, demographic groups, and individual users. Our findings suggest that this user-driven evaluation strategy can effectively identify AI model weaknesses that are not apparent in traditional benchmark evaluations.

In object detection, the decision-making process is crucial, and the conventional approach involves using a decision head that transforms the final feature map into bounding box coordinates and class labels. However, this method is limited by its reliance on a single decision head, which may not be able to handle complex objects effectively. To address this issue, we propose a novel multi-head decision network that leverages multiple decision heads to capture different aspects of objects. Our approach includes a multi-head design that can handle various object complexities and a multi-head attention mechanism that enables the network to focus on the most relevant decision head. Experimental results on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms the conventional approach and achieves state-of-the-art results.

Recent advancements in adversarial training have been hindered by a significant issue known as catastrophic overfitting, where models trained to withstand attacks become overly specialized and fail to generalize to clean data and various attacks. This issue has been attributed to the fact that the adversarial training process is inherently non-convex, making it difficult to optimize. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach that incorporates a convex optimization technique to tackle the non-convex nature of the problem. By employing a novel method that involves a two-stage optimization process, we are able to achieve a better balance between the model's ability to withstand attacks and its ability to generalize to clean data. Our proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective in practice, as it achieves superior performance on multiple datasets and attacks compared to existing methods.

Thakurta black holes are unique, rotating black holes that form from Kerr black holes when they interact with matter in a specific way. This interaction causes the matter to be drawn in and form an accretion disk, which then gets pushed away from the black hole. This process can lead to the formation of a stationary, rotating black hole known as a Thakurta black hole. Our research focuses on the conditions necessary for the formation of these black holes, and we find that they can only form in extremely rare situations. We also explore the properties of the Thakurta black hole, including its shape and how it behaves when it interacts with other objects. Our findings suggest that the existence of Thakurta black holes is highly unlikely, and we conclude that they are probably not present in the universe.

This study explores the impact of continuously changing goals on optimization algorithms that operate in real-time. We examine the behavior of a specific algorithm, known as the continuous-time subgradient method, when used for solving problems involving multiple objectives. Our analysis reveals that this approach can lead to suboptimal results, even in relatively simple scenarios. To address this issue, we propose a new method that involves adjusting the algorithm's speed based on the changing goals. We demonstrate through both theoretical and practical examples that this adaptation can improve the algorithm's performance.

A technology known as bootstrapping has become essential for homomorphic encryption, allowing for the execution of lengthy computations on encrypted data. However, the process of bootstrapping is plagued by a significant performance bottleneck, which hinders its practical application. To address this limitation, researchers have developed a new homomorphic encryption scheme that significantly reduces the bootstrapping time. The proposed scheme leverages a unique property of the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem to achieve this goal. The key to this innovation lies in the ability to use a small modulus for ciphertexts, which enables the use of a more efficient bootstrapping process. The proposed scheme has been shown to achieve a substantial reduction in the bootstrapping time, with a 10-fold improvement over existing schemes. The proposed scheme has been implemented using a software-based approach, which has been shown to achieve a 10-fold reduction in the bootstrapping time. The proposed scheme has been evaluated using a variety of benchmarks, including the evaluation of a polynomial of degree 100, the evaluation of a matrix multiplication of size 100x100, and the evaluation of a program that computes the Euclidean distance between two points. The results of these experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme in achieving a 10-fold reduction in the bootstrapping time.

We examine a specific type of random matrix ensemble, characterized by a rotationally invariant structure and a confining potential that grows quadratically. The ensemble's properties are defined by a specific probability measure, and we investigate its behavior in the large N limit, where N is the matrix size. The large N limit is found to exhibit a specific form of the eigenvalue density, and we derive the large N behavior of the partition function and the matrix elements' correlation functions. The results are obtained using the method of saddle point approximation, and the findings are consistent with the expected properties of the large N limit.

Quantum correlations, such as entanglement, are crucial in quantum information processing, but they aren't the only possible correlations. High-dimensional systems can exhibit non-entangled correlations, known as PPT bound entangled states. This research explores the non-local properties of PPT bound entangled states in systems with more than three dimensions. We demonstrate that certain PPT bound entangled states can violate Bell's inequalities, contradicting the previously held belief that entanglement is equivalent to quantum correlations. This discovery has significant implications for the understanding of quantum correlations and their applications in quantum information processing.

Bell's theorem is often attributed to a conflict between local causality and factorizability, but in this context, we argue that local causality should be replaced by an even more fundamental principle, namely, absolute continuity, which is a measure of probability. This is because factorizability is actually a consequence of absolute continuity, not local causality, and it is also possible to have factorizability without local causality, as demonstrated by the non-factorizable models of Bell.

We introduce a novel approach for generating videos, where the generated video can be seamlessly extended beyond its initial duration. Unlike previous methods that synthesize videos frame by frame, our continuous video generator allows for smooth, uninterrupted video production. To achieve this, we develop a new framework that integrates a video diffusion model with a continuous-time framework. By leveraging the strengths of both, our model can generate high-quality videos at any desired duration, while maintaining temporal consistency. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on multiple datasets, where our model outperforms existing methods in terms of visual quality and temporal coherence.

Given a finite reductive symplectic space $V$, we consider a dual pair $(G_1, G_2)$ where $G_1$ and $G_2$ are subgroups of $Sp(V)$. The $\Theta$-correspondence between irreducible representations of $G_1$ and $G_2$ is examined. This paper establishes a condition for a non-zero local term in the $\Theta$-correspondence between a specific type of character and a tempered character, involving the central character $\nu$ and a non-trivial additive character of $V$.

The effectiveness of thermoluminescence dosimetry in quantifying exposure to ionizing radiation is significantly influenced by the characteristics of the materials used. This study examines the thermal behavior of a widely used dosimetry material, calcium fluoride doped with dysprosium, by analyzing its thermal properties and dielectric properties in the frequency range of 100 kHz to 10 MHz. This analysis is conducted in the context of a theoretical framework that considers the material's properties as a mixture of Debye and Schottky functions.

This paper investigates the existence and multiplicity of solutions for a double phase problem featuring a non-autonomous double phase term and a singular hyperelastic term. The proof leverages Ekeland's variational principle in conjunction with the Nehari manifold method.

A novel approach to assessing the performance of imaging systems has been developed, focusing on the contrast to noise ratio (CNR) of specific features within images. This study investigates the properties of CNR in relation to the modulation transfer function (MTF) and the noise power spectrum (NPS) of imaging systems, and how it can be used to evaluate the performance of digital radiography systems. The paper also introduces a method for calculating the ideal CNR (ICNR) of an imaging system, which can be used to compare the performance of different systems. This study demonstrates the application of ICNR in evaluating the performance of various digital radiography systems, including those with different detector technologies and geometries.

Machine learning practitioners frequently use post hoc explanation methods to make complex models more understandable. However, these methods can be unreliable, leading to potentially misleading conclusions. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that uses a verification framework to ensure the accuracy of post hoc explanations. Our method, known as Local Assumption Verification (LAV), assesses the validity of post hoc explanations by testing specific assumptions about the model's behavior. By employing LAV, we can identify and correct flaws in post hoc explanations, ultimately improving their reliability. Our experiments demonstrate that LAV can effectively verify post hoc explanations in various scenarios, including those with noisy data and complex models.

Neural networks are often used to make predictions, but their decision-making process is unclear. To address this, researchers have developed explanation methods, but they have a limitation in that they are only effective when the model is slightly perturbed. We propose a new approach that provides explanations for neural networks that are not limited by this issue. We achieve this by training an interpretable model to replicate the neural network's behavior, using a technique called distillation. We show that this approach can replicate the neural network's performance and provide an interpretable explanation that can be easily understood by humans.

The compound displays a paramagnetic behavior at high temperatures, which transitions into a ferromagnetic state at 0.28 K. This article presents a family of long-lasting convex solution models to the power-of-mean curvature flow equation, valid for all p values exceeding 1/2, in a two-dimensional setting. These models, which are invariant under scaling transformations, are derived from a novel approach involving the construction of ancient solutions with a specific scaling symmetry. A key aspect of this work involves establishing a novel type of compactness for ancient solutions to the equation, which is valid for all p values exceeding 1/2, thereby enabling the derivation of curvature estimates and facilitating the construction of long-lasting solutions.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, yet their computational complexity and numerous parameters pose a significant challenge. To address this issue, we introduce a simplified version of the convolutional layer, known as the element-wise convolutional layer (ECLayer), which replaces the traditional convolution operation with a more efficient element-wise multiplication in the frequency domain. By doing so, ECLayer can be implemented using a single layer, thereby reducing the number of parameters and computational requirements. To further enhance the performance of ECLayer, we propose the use of multiple ECLayers with distinct frequency transformations, which can be efficiently implemented using the fast Fourier transform. Experimental results demonstrate that ECLayer can achieve comparable performance to traditional CNNs while significantly reducing the number of parameters and computational complexity.

Deep clustering methods have been extensively researched in recent years, yet they often rely on a single layer of representation, overlooking the potential benefits of multi-layer representations. This paper presents a novel deep clustering approach that effectively utilizes multi-layer representations, thereby enhancing the model's ability to capture complex patterns. By incorporating a multi-layer attention mechanism, the proposed method can dynamically weigh the importance of different layers, thereby improving the overall clustering performance. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Effective risk management is a critical component of organizational success, and it's vital to establish a robust risk identification process that's both comprehensive and adaptable. This study presents a novel, data-driven approach to risk identification, leveraging a sophisticated framework that integrates machine learning and natural language processing techniques. By analyzing a vast dataset of news articles, the system can automatically detect emerging risks and provide actionable insights to organizations. The proposed approach was tested using a real-world case study, and it demonstrated its ability to identify risks accurately and efficiently. The results indicate that this method can significantly enhance an organization's risk management capabilities, and it's poised to become a standard tool for risk management professionals.

This research paper introduces a novel classification approach rooted in the field of Topological Data Analysis (TDA). By leveraging persistent homology, it extracts key topological features from data, which are then used to inform the classification process. A novel classifier is proposed, which incorporates these topological features to enhance classification accuracy. Through experimentation on both artificial and real-world datasets, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to established classifiers.

We introduce a novel, non-similar approach called contrasimilarity, which deviates from traditional similarity-based methods by focusing on differences. This concept is applied to the study of processes, particularly in the context of labelled transition systems. We establish the relationship between contrasimilarity and similarity, demonstrating that they are duals of one another. Furthermore, we establish a connection between contrasimilarity and simulation, showing that it is the dual of the latter. We also prove that the contrasimilarity preorder is a bisimulation preorder. Additionally, we show that the contrasimilarity relation is preserved under the tensor product of processes, which is a key operation in the study of concurrent processes.

We've established a connection between the string 2-group and a specific mathematical structure, which we've used to create a functor that maps string 2-groups to a particular type of mathematical structure, denoted as $\mathbf{String}$. This functor, denoted as $\mathbf{String}$, is defined up to a specific equivalence and is unique in that it maps the string 2-group to its corresponding object. This equivalence is demonstrated by showing that the image of $\mathbf{String}$ is equivalent to the frame bundle of a string manifold, which is a key concept in mathematical physics.

The primary focus of this research lies in the investigation of modulational instability and rogue waves associated with solitary ion-acoustic waves in a plasma consisting of inertial ions and non-thermal electrons. The plasma's fundamental parameters significantly impact the key characteristics of ion-acoustic waves, including its modulational instability and rogue wave formation. The study's findings are validated through comparisons with numerical simulations.

Theoretical models of Alfvén waves in plasmas have been studied for decades, but their existence has only recently been confirmed in laboratory experiments. This study presents the first-ever direct observations of these waves in a specific type of plasma device, specifically in a spherical configuration. The experiment involved exciting the waves using a specific type of electrical signal and measuring their behavior using specific diagnostic tools. The results show that the waves propagate in a specific direction and have a specific frequency, which matches theoretical predictions. The study also found that the waves have a significant impact on the plasma's behavior, causing it to oscillate in a specific way. The findings of this study have important implications for our understanding of plasma behavior and have potential applications in various fields, including fusion energy research.

The presence of a magnetic field in a molecular cloud filament can lead to the growth of an instability, causing the cloud to fragment into smaller parts. This process is influenced by the cloud's internal pressure and its interaction with the surrounding magnetic field. In a study of this phenomenon, researchers have found that the cloud's growth rate and the size of its fragments are affected by the presence of ambipolar diffusion, a process in which the magnetic field and gas interact. By considering the effects of ambipolar diffusion, the researchers have derived a new equation that describes the growth of the cloud's instability, and have found that the presence of ambipolar diffusion can lead to the growth of shorter and more numerous fragments. This has important implications for understanding the formation of stars in a molecular cloud, and may help to explain why the cloud's fragments tend to be smaller than expected.

We examine the impact of periodic measurements on the speed of a quantum system's evolution, specifically in the context of a quantum spin chain with a specific Hamiltonian. By using the transfer matrix method, we derive a formula for the probability of the system remaining in its initial state after multiple measurements. We then investigate the speed of the system's evolution, both with and without measurements, and find that under certain conditions, repeated measurements can accelerate the system's evolution, resulting in the quantum Zeno effect and anti-Zeno effect.

We investigate the impact of magnetic field direction on the quantum coherence of a two-spin system, which is coupled through anisotropic interactions and subjected to external driving forces. Our analysis reveals that quantum coherence is influenced by the direction of the measurement basis relative to the interaction forces. Notably, coherent states can be sustained indefinitely under specific conditions, including the absence of external driving forces. Conversely, the application of external driving forces can lead to the generation of coherent states, which can be maintained for a finite period.

This study presents a novel approach to trajectory planning for multiple agents, 
leveraging a basic corridor concept to ensure collision-free movement. 
The proposed method, which is computationally efficient, can be applied in real-time 
and is demonstrated through simulations on complex scenarios involving multiple 
agents, showcasing its ability to generate collision-free paths.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) has been extensively researched in the field of autonomous driving, particularly in the context of lane detection. However, existing methods have limitations due to the inherent differences between the source and target domains, which hinder the transfer of knowledge. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages a self-supervised mechanism to bridge the gap between the two domains. By utilizing a self-training strategy, our method can effectively learn domain-invariant features and reduce the discrepancy between the two domains. To further enhance the quality of pseudo-labels, we propose a self-training framework that combines a self-training module and a consistency module. The self-training module generates pseudo-labels for the target domain, while the consistency module ensures that the pseudo-labels are consistent across different views of the same image. To improve the accuracy of the pseudo-labels, we also propose a pseudo-label refinement module that refines the pseudo-labels based on the consistency module. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on the CULane and TuSimple datasets.

The behavior of water droplets on superabsorbent polymers is heavily influenced by the physical and chemical properties of the polymers, which can be manipulated by adjusting the concentration of the adsorbed particles. This study investigates the effect of varying the concentration of the particles on the dynamics of water droplets on polymer surfaces. By analyzing the absorption time of the droplets, we found that the absorption time increases with higher particle concentrations, which is attributed to a decrease in the swelling rate of the polymers. This phenomenon is further explained by the fact that an increase in particle concentration leads to a decrease in the polymer's mesh size, which in turn affects the diffusion of water molecules into the polymer. This research provides valuable insights into the behavior of water droplets on polymer surfaces and has potential applications in various fields, including drug delivery and environmental remediation.

In educational settings, collaborative learning is often seen as a positive factor for student engagement and learning outcomes. However, research has shown that the relationship between student collaboration and performance is complex and influenced by various contextual factors. A recent study examined the relationship between student collaboration and performance in a large-scale introductory Python course, analyzing the context of the course, the students, and the platform used for collaboration. The results revealed that the relationship between student collaboration and performance is influenced by the course's context, the students' characteristics, and the platform used. These findings highlight the importance of considering multiple contextual factors when evaluating collaborative learning and suggest that interventions to promote student collaboration should be tailored to the specific context in which they are implemented.

Radar Wind Profilers are a widely used tool for measuring wind speed and direction in the lower atmosphere, and they're also being increasingly applied to the upper atmosphere. These devices use Doppler shifts in scattered signals to determine wind speed and direction, but they can be affected by errors due to the presence of multiple types of scatterers. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new method for analyzing data from co-located RWP and GPS radio occultation systems. This method uses a technique called Kalman filtering to correct for errors in RWP measurements, and it has been successfully applied to data collected by the Canadian RWP network and the GPS radio occultation system. The results show that the corrected RWP measurements are in good agreement with the GRPO measurements, and that the corrected data can be used to improve the accuracy of atmospheric models.

A binary star system, consisting of a white dwarf and a red giant, has been discovered in the globular cluster NGC 6396. The system's binary nature was confirmed through spectroscopic observations, and its orbital characteristics were determined using radial velocity measurements. The system's binary orbit has a period of approximately 1.3 years and a high eccentricity of 0.93, making it the most eccentric binary system known in a globular cluster. The system's binary nature has implications for understanding the formation of binary systems in dense star clusters. The system's binary orbit has a high eccentricity, which suggests that it may have formed through a specific process involving the interaction of stars in the cluster. In the absence of high-quality parallel data, researchers can still generate synthetic translations using machine translation systems. This study explores the potential of such synthetic data in enhancing text mining tasks, specifically by improving reference translations. We investigate whether synthetic translations can be effectively used to correct inaccuracies in existing parallel data, and in doing so, we examine the quality of these synthetic translations in comparison to human-created equivalents. We also examine whether incorporating synthetic data can improve the performance of text mining tasks, and in our experiments, we find that synthetic translations can indeed correct errors in reference translations, and that they can be effectively used to improve the quality of these references.

In our research, we investigate the entanglement growth in a quantum system composed of two interacting parts, one evolving under unitary rules and the other under dissipative processes. By analyzing the behavior of the system in both scenarios, we find that when the dissipative component is a small fraction of the system, the entanglement increases at a rate proportional to the system size. However, when the unitary component is the dominant factor, the entanglement follows a logarithmic scaling pattern. Our findings are based on a specific model where the two dynamics interact in a controlled manner, and we use a combination of analytical and numerical methods to validate our results.

Using a combination of theoretical models and computational methods, we investigate the impact of an external electric field on the interlayer interactions and band structure of transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers. By applying the screened interaction model and density functional theory, we find that a perpendicular electric field can significantly alter the interlayer hybridization, leading to the emergence of a bandgap in the heterobilayers. This effect is further analyzed through the density functional theory, which reveals that a perpendicular electric field can induce a substantial change in the band structure, including the appearance of a new bandgap. The results of our study provide valuable insights into the tunability of band structure in transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers and its potential applications in optoelectronic devices.

Recent advancements in quantum computing have led to the development of quantum computing systems capable of efficiently processing complex tasks. A notable example is the echo state network, a quantum computing model that has shown promise in solving intricate problems. Researchers have successfully applied this model to various quantum systems, including those based on bosonic and fermionic states. In this study, we investigate the echo state property in a broader range of quantum systems, including qubit-based reservoir computing systems. Our research reveals that the necessary and sufficient conditions for these systems to exhibit the echo state property are related to the behavior of their eigenvalues. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the echo state property holds for a wide variety of quantum systems, including those based on bosonic and fermionic states, as well as those with complex eigenvalue distributions. Our findings have significant implications for the development of quantum computing systems, as they provide a deeper understanding of the conditions required for these systems to exhibit the echo state property.

The development of photonic integrated circuits has been hindered by the lack of suitable on-chip quantum memory. Trapped single atoms, however, can serve as such memory, offering long coherence times and efficient interaction with light. We have successfully created a hybrid photon-atom integrated circuit using a single rubidium atom, trapped in a 2D optical dipole trap, and a silicon nitride waveguide. The system enables the deterministic generation of single photons and their coupling to the waveguide, achieving a high efficiency of 1.5% in photon emission and demonstrating the feasibility of this approach for large-scale quantum information processing.

This study introduces two finite element approaches for the Laplace equation that are based on a newly developed concept of weighted averaging. These methods can be seen as a continuation of a 2018 publication by the same authors, which focused on the Poisson equation. The proposed formulations are versatile and can be applied to any type of finite element, including those that are not conforming. The methods are rigorously analyzed for stability and convergence. Additionally, the numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of these approaches in practice.

This research paper introduces a novel approach to modeling the propagation of acoustic waves through complex fluid environments containing numerous bubbles. The proposed method is founded on a stochastic representation of the bubble distribution, which is then used to derive a probabilistic description of the acoustic wave's behavior. By applying the stochastic Fokker-Planck equation, we establish a framework for simulating the acoustic wave's interaction with bubble clusters, and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments. The results show that the presence of microbubbles significantly amplifies pressure levels in the surrounding area, and the proposed method provides a more accurate description of this phenomenon compared to existing models.

Human emotions are significantly impacted by stress, which can be detrimental to both mental and physical health. This study examines the relationship between emotional expression and stress levels in individuals, using a dataset of facial images captured from individuals undergoing stress tests. By applying deep learning techniques, we have developed a method to quantify emotional intensity and stress levels in individuals, and have demonstrated its effectiveness in predicting emotional responses to various stimuli. Our results show that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of accuracy and robustness, and have the potential to be used in a range of applications, including emotion recognition and stress management.

We introduce PanGEA, a user-friendly and efficient annotation tool designed for annotating spatial navigation tasks, including directions and routes, with both visual and written descriptions. PanGEA can accommodate various annotation types, such as landmarks, destinations, and textual annotations, and can be easily adapted to different platforms, such as mobile devices and VR environments. PanGEA's modular design and user-friendly interface make it a flexible and scalable solution for annotating diverse navigation tasks, and its source code is freely available on GitHub.
